Accuracy of a hot-spot map

Source: R/hsacc.R
hsacc.Rd

Asks how well a map of predicted hot spots (from kdsurf(), prohs(), rtmfit() or any score per cell) caught the crimes that followed. The hot cells are those of highest predicted score whose areas together first reach the share top of the study area (or the cells marked TRUE when pred is logical). Then:

Usage

hsacc(pred, obs, area = NULL, top = 0.1, prev = NULL, ties = "in")

Arguments

pred

The predicted score of each cell (higher is hotter), or TRUE for the cells of a map's hot spots.

obs

The crimes of each cell in the evaluation period: numbers from 0, not all 0.

area

NULL for cells of equal area, or the area of each cell: positive.

top

The shares of the area to mark hot: numbers above 0 and at most 1, one row of the result each (not read when pred is logical).

prev

NULL or the crimes of each cell in the period the map was made from: numbers from 0.

ties

Which of the cells whose score ties across the cut-off of top are hot: "in" (the default) all of them, so that the hot area may pass top; "out" none of them, so that it may fall short; or "frac" each by the share of their area that the cut-off still needs, so that the hot area is top and cells, area, n and nmax may be fractional. The sources cited do not say how ties are broken. With any of the three the result does not depend on the order of the cells; with no tie across the cut-off all three give the first cells by score whose areas reach top, as before ties was added (when ties were broken by position, so that reordering the cells could change the result).

Value

A data frame with one row per top: top, cells, area (hot), ashare, n, N, hit, pai, nmax, pei and rri (NA without prev).

Details

  • the hit rate n / N, the share of the crimes of the evaluation period (obs) in hot cells, and the predictive accuracy index PAI = (n / N) / (a / A), the hit rate over the hot share of the area (Chainey, Tompson and Uhlig 2008);

  • the predictive efficiency index PEI = n / nmax, the crimes caught over the most an area of the same size could have caught, its cells taken by observed crimes per unit area, of equal density the larger first (Drawve 2016): 1 for a perfect map of that size;

  • with prev, the counts of the period the map was made from, the recapture rate index of Levine (2008), (n / n_prev) / (N / N_prev): whether the hot cells kept their crimes better than the whole area.

References

Chainey, S., Tompson, L. and Uhlig, S. (2008). The utility of hotspot mapping for predicting spatial patterns of crime. Security Journal, 21(1-2), 4-28. doi:10.1057/palgrave.sj.8350066

Levine, N. (2008). The "hottest" part of a hotspot: comments on "The utility of hotspot mapping for predicting spatial patterns of crime". Security Journal, 21(4), 295-302. doi:10.1057/sj.2008.5

Drawve, G. (2016). A metric comparison of predictive hot spot techniques and RTM. Justice Quarterly, 33(3), 369-397. doi:10.1080/07418825.2014.904393

Examples

set.seed(12)
risk <- rgamma(400, 0.5)
before <- rpois(400, risk)
after <- rpois(400, risk)
hsacc(pred = before, obs = after, top = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2), prev = before)
#>    top cells area ashare   n   N       hit      pai nmax       pei       rri
#> 1 0.05    42   42  0.105  59 177 0.3333333 3.174603  110 0.5363636 0.5451713
#> 2 0.10    42   42  0.105  59 177 0.3333333 3.174603  110 0.5363636 0.5451713
#> 3 0.20   110  110  0.275 107 177 0.6045198 2.198254  177 0.6045198 0.6045198
